name: Lateral pontine syndrome (AICA infarct)
presentation: A patient develops sudden vertigo and vomiting with deafness in one ear, a complete facial palsy on the same side, and clumsiness of the arm and leg on that side. Pain sensation is lost on that side of the face and on the opposite side of the body, and there may be a Horner syndrome. Weakness is absent. It looks like a Wallenberg syndrome that has moved up one level and acquired the seventh and eighth nerves.

deficits.sign: Sudden sensorineural deafness (cochlear nucleus, labyrinthine artery)
Ataxia from the middle cerebellar peduncle and cerebellar infarct
Facial pain and temperature loss (spinal trigeminal tract)
Body pain and temperature loss (spinothalamic tract)

reasoning: The anterior inferior cerebellar artery supplies the lateral caudal pons, the middle cerebellar peduncle, the anterior inferior cerebellum and, through the labyrinthine artery, the inner ear. The lateral pontine tegmentum contains the same long tracts that make the lateral medullary syndrome, the spinothalamic tract (already crossed, so body pain loss is contralateral), the spinal trigeminal tract (uncrossed, so facial pain loss is ipsilateral) and the descending sympathetic fibers (uncrossed, giving an ipsilateral Horner), plus the structures specific to this level: the facial motor nucleus, the cochlear and vestibular nuclei at the pontomedullary junction and the middle cerebellar peduncle. These are all ipsilateral, so the facial palsy, deafness, vertigo and ataxia are on the side of the lesion. The corticospinal fibers in the basis pontis and the medial lemniscus lie in the paramedian territory of the basilar perforators and are spared, hence no weakness or proprioceptive loss. Deafness is the distinguishing feature: an isolated acute unilateral hearing loss with vertigo should always raise AICA infarction, since the labyrinthine artery is usually a branch of AICA.

imagingFindings.finding: Restricted diffusion in the lateral caudal pons, middle cerebellar peduncle and anterior inferior cerebellum (flocculus region).
Basilar atherosclerosis at the AICA origin or AICA occlusion; vertebrobasilar dissection in the young.

commonCauses: Basilar artery atherosclerosis occluding the AICA origin

mimics.name: Vestibular neuritis with a coincidental Bell palsy
mimics.howToDistinguish: No deafness, no crossed sensory loss, no ataxia beyond imbalance

mimics.name: Lateral medullary syndrome
mimics.howToDistinguish: No deafness or facial palsy; dysphagia and hoarseness present

mimics.name: Labyrinthitis
mimics.howToDistinguish: Hearing loss and vertigo with normal neurological examination and negative DWI

management: Stroke treatment; anticoagulate for dissection or cardioembolism as appropriate
Eye protection for the facial palsy; vestibular rehabilitation

imagingHint.label: lateral caudal pons and middle cerebellar peduncle
